Date: 2026-05-07
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Location: Redwood In-Studio (recording) / Zoom fallback
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood Marketing), Daniel Park (Emberly CTO), Amira Gomez (Emberly Head of Product), Lewis Hart (Emberly ML)
summary: A semi-structured in-studio testimonial recording with Emberly focusing on the performance and operational improvements since migrating inference to Redwood. Conversation covers integration timeline, cost/latency impact, reliability stories, and customer-facing outcomes. Audio will be edited for a short podcast and a one-page case study; Emberly to approve quotes and headshots.

Quotes for case study and podcast edits
transcript:
[00:00:00] Priya (Marketing): All right, welcome everybody—this is the Redwood podcast-style testimonial with Emberly. Were recording live in-studio and on Zoom. Quick audio check, can you hear me Daniel?
[00:00:08] Daniel (Emberly CTO): Yep loud and clear, thanks.
[00:00:11] Lena (AE): Great. Im Lena from Redwood, Ill kick off with a couple of warm-up questions then hand off to Marcus for a few tech bits.
[00:00:19] Marcus (SE): Hey everyone. Hi Amira, Lewis. Thanks for joining—well keep this conversational.
[00:00:25] Daniel: Thanks for having us. Were excited.
[00:00:28] Priya: Cool. First question for Daniel: in one sentence, what problem were you trying to solve that made you evaluate Redwood?
[00:00:38] Daniel: Uh, sure—so Emberly runs a realtime content personalization engine and we were struggling with token latency variability and spotty p99 spikes at peak. We needed predictable costs too; the cloud provider approach became way too expensive once we scaled.
[00:00:56] Lena: And how long was the evaluation and pilot?
[00:00:59] Daniel: From kickoff to pilot was... roughly six weeks. We did a small production pilot for three weeks, then rolled to 40% traffic for another two.
[00:01:12] Amira (Head of Product): I can add—we had a stakeholder group: product, infra, legal. We needed clarity on data residency and audit trails as well.
[00:01:22] Marcus: Thats great context. Can you share the top two metrics you care about now, post migration?
[00:01:29] Daniel: P50 latency went from ~160ms down to 42ms, p99 from 1.2s to about 180ms on our critical endpoints. Cost per 1k tokens dropped by nearly 45% after we switched quantization/profile suggested by Redwood Optimize.
[00:01:49] Lewis (ML Eng): The caching improvements also knocked out a bunch of repetitive tokens—prefix caching saved us compute for repeated prompts. Sometimes those micro-savings add up a lot.
[00:01:59] Priya: Nice, those are great sound bites. Marcus, do you want to sketch the technical migration at a high level for the listeners?
[00:02:08] Marcus: Yeah. Emberly had their model fleet on a managed endpoint—VMs running a mix of frameworks. We onboarded the model to Redwood Dedicated with minor conversion steps; our runtime picked optimized kernels, we enabled continuous batching and prefix/KV caching. For Emberlys sequences the throughput gains were immediate.
[00:02:28] Daniel: There were a couple of tricky bits—our feature store ties to internal user IDs and we had to ensure no PII left the VPC. Redwoods Private option and the KMS integration made that flow smoother, though there were a few audit questions initially.
[00:02:41] Marcus: Right, and we worked with Lewis to set up KMS policies and rotate keys; some of the docs refer to "Redwood Consul" in the transcript but the product is Redwood Console—docs sometimes misread the name but the team understood.
[00:02:54] Priya: (laughs) Will note that in editing. One candid area people want to hear about: incidents or reliability—did you have any significant outages during the rollout?
[00:03:05] Amira: We had one incident where an autoscaling policy misfired during a campaign spike and we hit a throttling safety net. Marcus and the on-call SEs worked with our infra team; fallback routing to a slightly smaller model kept the service alive. That incident actually proved the value of the routing/fallback policies.
[00:03:26] Daniel: Exactly—business continued, no notable customer impact, and the postmortem was quick.
[00:03:31] Lena: Thats a solid reliability story. Can you speak to developer experience—was integration easy for your engineers?
[00:03:39] Lewis: Yes, the SDKs were clean; we pushed a compatibility shim in a day and then traded with Marcus on tokenization edge cases. The dev workflow felt familiar which reduced friction.
[00:03:50] Marcus: There were a few small transcription mismatches in the docs—example: "KV cache" sometimes read as "K V cash" in a generated doc. Sorry about that to future readers, but its manageable.
[00:04:01] Priya: (smiles) okay audio-quirk notes aside, for the case study wed love a concrete quote about business impact. Daniel, can you give a 1-2 sentence quote?
[00:04:12] Daniel: Sure. "Switching to Redwood reduced latency and cost materially while giving us the confidence to serve peak traffic without manual ops babysitting".
[00:04:22] Priya: Perfect. Well refine that wording with you before publishing.
[00:04:27] [00:04:30] Marcus: Quick technical note—Emberly also adopted a 4-bit quantized model for some batch workloads. We recommended a mixed strategy: quantized for non-customer-facing batch, full-precision for live personalization. That hybrid plan cut cost without material quality loss.
[00:04:46] Lewis: Yep, and we did A/B tests to ensure downstream CTR didnt drop. It actually improved in some cohorts.
[00:04:54] Priya: Nice anecdote. Switching lenses: security & compliance—what did legal or infosec ask for and how did Redwood help?
[00:05:03] Amira: The checklist was SOC2, SAML SSO, audit logs, and KMS integration. Redwood provided the SOC2 attestation and a sample SAML config; the audit logs in Redwood Console were helpful during our internal review. There was minor doc confusion about retention windows but that got sorted.
[00:05:20] Lena: Good to hear. Did you run any independent benchmarks or share logs with Redwood during the pilot?
[00:05:26] Daniel: We shared a small benchmark harness and Redwood ran parallel tests; that gave us confidence the numbers were reproducible.
[00:05:33] [00:05:35] Priya: For the podcast edit we want a short story arc—problem, solution, outcome—what would you say is the human outcome? Any customer quote about what this meant to product or ops teams?
[00:05:46] Amira: For product, the outcome was faster iteration; the team could try a personalization experiment and see results within a day. For ops, the relieve—less late-night pager—was tangible. One of our PMs said, "we shipped with barely a meeting" which is a little dramatic but mostly true.
[00:06:03] Priya: I love that. Well probably use "barely a meeting" in the headline.
[00:06:06] Daniel: (laughs) fine with it.
[00:06:09] Lena: Curious—any surprises post-migration? Things you didn't expect?
[00:06:14] Lewis: Two surprises: first, the KV/prefix caching edge cases where some long-tail prompts didn't cache as we expected; that required a small prompt rewrite. Second, our cost model improved more than we'd forecast because Redwoods batching behaved better under real traffic patterns than synthetic tests suggested.
[00:06:32] Marcus: We do sometimes see better real-world gains because batching benefits compound with request patterns.
[00:06:38] [00:06:40] Priya: Alright were getting great content. A few quick rapid-fire questions for color: favorite Redwood feature?
[00:06:48] Daniel: Smart routing—being able to route by region and cost tier was huge.
[00:06:52] Amira: The Console dashboards—those token-level cost views helped us explain ROI to finance.
[00:06:57] Lewis: The SDK and the latency profiles were most useful dev-side.
[00:07:02] Lena: Any vendor comparisons during selection, and why Redwood won?
[00:07:06] Daniel: We evaluated Anthropics managed endpoints and self-hosting on GPUs. Anthropic felt simpler but pricier, self-hosting demanded too much infra work. Redwood hit the sweet spot of performance and manageability.
[00:07:20] [00:07:25] Priya: We always appreciate the honesty. For the case study visuals, can you provide usage numbers we can put on the one-pager? Specifics are helpful but keep anything sensitive out—just percent improvements and timelines.
[00:07:37] Amira: We can share percentages: 45% cost reduction per 1k tokens, p99 improved by ~85%, and time-to-production from pilot to 40% roll was under 8 weeks.
[00:07:52] Priya: Great. We may round the numbers for the public piece.
[00:07:55] [00:08:00] Marcus: Small technical aside—during the initial pilot we observed a small mismatch in tokenization between Emberly's tokenizer and the model tokenizer. Lewis helped by adding a shim in the frontend that normalized spaces. Little fixes like that save a lot of trouble later.
[00:08:16] Lewis: Thats true—tokenization mismatches show up in unpredictable ways.
[00:08:20] [00:08:25] Priya: Moving toward wrap-up: any recommendations for teams thinking about a similar migration? Short list—what would you tell them?
[00:08:33] Daniel: Have a clear pilot with traffic mirroring, validate p99 and tail latency, and include legal early for KMS/retention questions.
[00:08:43] Amira: Add a short prompt audit as part of the migration plan—prompt rewrites can salvage caching efficiency.
[00:08:49] Lewis: And build a small telemetry dashboard early to monitor token distribution and batching effectiveness.
[00:08:56] [00:09:00] Priya: Perfect. Well chase a few final production details off-line. Lena, any commercial notes we should record for the case study?
[00:09:08] Lena: Just that Emberly is on a Dedicated plan with a Reserved capacity contract; were working on a follow-on optimization engagement. None of the commercial specifics for public copy without approval.
[00:09:21] Daniel: Sounds good.
[00:09:24] [00:09:30] Priya: Okay last fun question for the podcast: whats a feature you wish existed? Something a bit human.
[00:09:36] Daniel: Id love a human-friendly cost-forecasting tool that explains why a spike happened in plain English.
[00:09:44] Amira: A button that says "make the model a little faster"—obviously joking but a higher-level knob would be handy.
[00:09:51] [00:09:55] Priya: (laughs) Well put that in the wish list. Alright, were going to record a short outro with Daniel for a neat quote and then well stop.
[00:10:02] Daniel: Go for it.
[00:10:05] [00:10:07] Priya: (microphone) Daniel, final line for the podcast—what should listeners take away?
[00:10:12] Daniel: "If youre scaling personalized experiences, invest in an inference strategy that prioritizes predictable latency and cost—those two things unlock product velocity."
[00:10:21] Priya: Beautiful. Thank you. End of recording.
